title: Threat Modeling Fundamentals

lesson.text: You cannot secure what you do not see.

Attack surface defined: every point where an attacker can interact with a system. Village framing — gates, walls, sewer grates, fords — and their digital equivalents: endpoints, APIs, login forms, forgotten admin panels.
Defense-in-Depth — layered PREVENTATIVE (stop), DETERRENT (discourage), and DETECTIVE (observe & alert) controls. A system relying on prevention alone fails silently.
Some controls blur — a barking dog both deters AND alerts. Classify by the control's PRIMARY purpose, and when in doubt ask: does it STOP the act, or RECORD it?

Capability mapping: real threat modeling defends against the SPECIFIC actors capable of exploiting SPECIFIC gaps, not "everyone." Reference the Saboteur: high dexterity and stealth versus an unwatched lock on a cliff path.
In the field you'll find this as the West Gate. In an audit you'll find it as an unlogged service endpoint behind a default password.

brief: The Herald wants the western perimeter audited before nightfall, Agent. Two points need a real control assigned — not just any control, but the one that actually holds under pressure. Place your choice, then watch what happens when it's tested.

slots.label: The Castle Approach — a moat, an iron gate, and a guardpost. Every visitor passes through in daylight, under watch. Assign the control that gives the Division a record of who came and went.

consequence.moat: Called to account after an incident, the guard captain can only say the moat kept casual wanderers back — it holds no memory of who actually crossed the drawbridge.
consequence.iron_gate: Called to account after an incident, the guard captain can only say the gate was shut when it should've been — it holds no memory of who walked through while it was open.
consequence.logbook: Called to account after an incident, the guard captain hands over a name and a time — the Division knows exactly who came through, and when.

explain.moat: Preventative — a physical barrier that stops the approach before it starts.
explain.iron_gate: Preventative — an access barrier that stops entry before it starts.
explain.logbook: Detective — the logbook records and reveals who came, enabling audit after the fact.

slots.hint: Ignore what each control looks like doing — ask only which one leaves a record you'd check AFTER the fact, not before.

variant.label: The Vault Door — reinforced steel, a silent alarm wired to motion sensors, and a guard who's been bribed to look away. Assign the control that actually tells the Division a breach happened.

consequence.steel_door: The door holds — until someone with the right tools spends an afternoon on it. Nothing about a locked door tells you that afternoon happened.
consequence.silent_alarm: The door gives way eventually, but the moment motion crosses the vault floor, the alarm is already ringing at the guardhouse.
consequence.bribed_guard: The guard waves the intruder straight through and reports nothing — this was never a control, just a paid-off liability.

explain.steel_door: Preventative — a physical barrier that stops entry before it starts.
explain.silent_alarm: Detective — the alarm doesn't stop anyone; it alerts you that someone got past the door.
explain.bribed_guard: This one's compromised, not a control at all — a bribed guard enforces nothing.

slots.label: The Cliff Path Lock — an unwatched gap on a high, narrow ledge. The Herald's scouts report a Saboteur nearby: high dexterity, high stealth, patient. Assign the control that actually stops him, specifically.

consequence.stronger_lock: The Saboteur spends a patient hour on the lock and walks through — an unwatched path doesn't care how good your lock is if no one is ever there to notice it failed.
consequence.guard_dog: A stealthy, patient professional reads the dog's patrol rhythm and slips through in the gap between rounds — deterrence only works on someone who can be scared off.
consequence.hidden_alarm: The lock gives eventually, exactly as the report warned it might — but the moment he's through, the alarm reaches the guardhouse before he's ten paces down the path.

explain.stronger_lock: Raw strength isn't what mattered here — the gap is a delicate lock, not a barred door, and a stronger lock still fails silently once picked.
explain.guard_dog: Threat modeling maps actor capability to system gap — a deterrent aimed at casual intruders is the wrong tool against high stealth and patience.
explain.hidden_alarm: Detective — even where prevention can't hold forever, a detective control means the breach doesn't happen invisibly.

slots.hint: The lesson's own rule applies here: prevention alone fails SILENTLY. Which option is the only one that leaves a trace if the Saboteur gets through?

capstoneQuestion.q: Your web app has a login page, a public API, and an old admin panel nobody remembers. Which is part of the attack surface?
explain: The attack surface isn't just the obvious front door.
The API matters, but it isn't the whole picture.
Attack surface = every interaction point, ESPECIALLY the forgotten ones — that is your West Gate.
